prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

On the birthday of the world I begin to contemplate what I have done and left undone, but this year not so much rebuilding of my perennially damaged psyche, shoring up eroding friendships, digging out stumps of old resentments that refuse to rot on their own. No, this year I want to call myself to task for what I have done and not done for peace. How much have I dared in opposition? How much have I put on the line for freedom? For mine and others? As these freedoms are pared, sliced and diced, where have I spoken out? Who have I tried to move? In this holy season, I stand self-convicted of sloth in a time when lies choke the mind and rhetoric bends reason to slithering choking pythons. Here I stand before the gates opening, the fire dazzling my eyes, and as I approach what judges me, I judge myself. Give me weapons of minute destruction. Let my words turn into sparks.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: How, For, Who

outputs.L1:
On the birthday of the world, I begin to contemplate what I have done and left undone. But this year, I am concerned less with rebuilding my perennially damaged psyche, shoring up eroding friendships, or digging out the stumps of old resentments that refuse to rot on their own. No, this year I want to call myself to account for what I have—and have not—done for peace. How greatly have I dared to oppose? How much have I put on the line for freedom—my own and that of others? As these freedoms are pared, sliced, and diced, where have I spoken out? Whom have I tried to move?

In this holy season, I stand self-convicted of sloth at a time when lies choke the mind and rhetoric twists reason into slithering, constricting pythons. Here I stand before the opening gates, the fire dazzling my eyes; and as I approach that which judges me, I judge myself.

Give me weapons of minute destruction. Let my words become sparks.
outputs.L2: On the world’s anniversary, I usually take stock of my actions and omissions. But this year, I am less concerned with repairing my chronically wounded spirit, reinforcing friendships worn thin, or uprooting ancient grudges that will not decay by themselves. Instead, I intend to answer for what I have—and have not—done in the cause of peace. How boldly have I resisted? What have I risked for liberty, both my own and that of others? As those liberties are trimmed, carved up, and diminished, when have I raised my voice? Whom have I sought to persuade? During this sacred season, I find myself guilty of idleness while falsehoods suffocate thought and language twists reason into writhing, strangling serpents. I wait before the opening gates, their flames blazing in my vision; and as I draw near to that which will pass judgment on me, I pass judgment on myself. Arm me with instruments of small-scale destruction. May my words ignite into embers.
outputs.L3:
The speaker treats the world’s birthday as an occasion for moral self-examination. Instead of dwelling on personal wounds or strained relationships, they turn their attention to a larger and more urgent concern: their failure to work hard enough for peace. They question whether they have opposed injustice with sufficient courage, defended freedom with enough determination, spoken out when silence was easier, or inspired others to take action.

This reflection leads to a painful condemnation of their own passivity in a world saturated with lies and manipulative rhetoric. The speaker recognizes that remaining silent or inactive can amount to complicity. Yet the reflection does not end in despair. Rather, it becomes a call to transform language into action. The speaker seeks to make words into small but powerful tools—capable of challenging falsehood, resisting oppression, and contributing to meaningful change.
outputs.L4:
Here is an original expanded version based on the summary:

On this birthday of the world, I find myself unable to celebrate without first taking account of my own silence. What have I done while freedoms have narrowed, while lies have dressed themselves as truth, and while polished voices have taught fear to sound like reason? I have watched, understood, objected in private—and too often mistaken awareness for courage.

I cannot accuse the age without also accusing myself. I have waited for others to speak first, for safer circumstances, for some unmistakable moment when resistance would demand less sacrifice. Complacency has been my shelter. I have accepted small losses of liberty because each seemed survivable, and I have allowed the language of power to define what was realistic, lawful, or inevitable.

But peace is not preserved by passivity, and freedom does not defend itself. Both depend upon people willing to interrupt the rehearsed story, expose deception, and imagine what authority insists is impossible. If I possess no army, office, or wealth, I still possess a voice. I still have words.

So I will use them—not as decorations, but as instruments; not to numb, but to awaken. Let them become “weapons of minute destruction,” breaking apart one falsehood, one fear, one obedient silence at a time. A sentence may be small, but it can enter where armies cannot. It can unsettle certainty, restore memory, and remind another person that they are not alone.

Today I resolve to speak more boldly for peace and freedom. I may not change the world by myself, but every refusal begins with an individual voice. Every resistance starts when someone names what is happening and another answers. If words can pass from mind to mind like sparks, then I will strike them while I can—and trust that somewhere, in someone, they will catch fire.
outputs.L5:
### How, For, Who

Every meaningful project begins with three questions: **How will it work? Who is it for? What purpose is it for?**

**How** focuses on the process. It encourages us to consider the tools, methods, and actions needed to turn an idea into reality.

**For** defines the purpose. A clear purpose guides decisions, establishes priorities, and explains why the work matters.

**Who** identifies the people involved. Understanding their needs, expectations, and experiences helps us create something relevant and valuable.

Together, **How, For, and Who** provide a simple framework for thoughtful planning. When we understand the process, purpose, and audience, we can make better decisions and achieve more meaningful results.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical first-person meditation for Rosh Hashanah in which the speaker examines not personal failings, but their failure to stand up for peace and freedom amid growing political repression.
counterfactuals.output:
At the turning of the year,  
I do not come only to number  
the careless word, the closed hand,  
the promise left undone.

I come to ask where I was  
when the doors narrowed,  
when truth learned to whisper,  
when neighbors lowered their eyes  
at the sound of boots, decrees,  
and names made dangerous.

The shofar does not let me hide.  
Its cry crosses every excuse.  
It asks not whether I kept myself innocent,  
but whether I kept faith  
with those whose freedom was taken  
piece by piece,  
while I mistook my silence for safety.

I have prayed for peace  
as though peace were weather—  
a blessing that might drift down  
if only I waited.

But peace is not passivity.  
Peace is the courage to refuse  
the order that degrades,  
the lie that divides,  
the fear that makes a prison  
of the public square.

I have cherished freedom  
as an inheritance  
and failed to guard it as a flame.  
I have watched the powerful  
rename cruelty as necessity,  
obedience as unity,  
and repression as calm.  
Too often, I answered  
with sorrow instead of speech,  
with private outrage  
instead of public witness.

Avinu Malkeinu,  
write me not into the book  
of the blameless—  
there is no such book.

Write me into the book  
of those who awaken.

Teach me that repentance  
is not only regret,  
but return:  
to the stranger at the gate,  
to the captive whose name I know,  
to the threatened voice,  
to the difficult work  
of standing beside another  
when standing has a cost.

May I not seek a peace  
built on someone else’s silence.  
May I not call myself free  
while another is forbidden  
to speak, to gather, to mourn,  
to hope aloud.

This year, let the shofar  
break the sleep of my caution.  
Let its long cry become breath in me—  
not hatred, not vengeance,  
but courage joined to mercy,  
truth joined to action.

At the threshold of the year,  
I ask for no clean slate.

I ask for a steadier hand,  
an unhidden voice,  
and the strength to make  
from repentance a door—

and to hold it open.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poetic prose passage about self-judgment at the Jewish New Year, using images of damaged friendships, buried resentment, choking lies, fire, and words becoming sparks.
counterfactuals.output:
At the Jewish New Year, before any heavenly court can open its books, I summon myself to judgment. I count the friendships left cracked at the edges, cups once shared now gathering dust; I dig through the hard earth of silence and uncover resentments I had buried alive. The lies I called mercy rise in my throat like smoke, choking every prayer before it can become breath.

The shofar sounds—not an answer, but an alarm. Somewhere within me, a fire has survived the year, feeding on old shame and unspoken blame. I must choose what it will consume. So I bring each word near the flame. Some blacken into ash; some lift as sparks—apology, forgiveness, return—small burning letters seeking the dark faces I have wronged. And as the year turns, I ask not to be declared innocent, only awake enough to begin again.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Imagine an activist reflecting during the High Holy Days: What have they risked for justice, whose freedom have they defended, and when have they remained silent? Write the reflection in urgent, metaphor-rich language.
counterfactuals.output:
The shofar does not ask whether I had good intentions.  
It tears the air open and asks: **What did you risk?**

Did I bring justice only what I could spare—  
an hour, a signature, a coin—  
or did I place my comfort on the altar?  
Did I step between the boot and the throat?  
Did I spend my name, my safety, my belonging,  
or guard them like idols while others paid in blood?

Whose freedom did I defend  
when the prison door was not mine,  
when the slur did not strike my body,  
when the law sharpened its teeth for someone else?  
Did I widen the circle of breath,  
or merely mourn after the air was gone?

And where was I silent?

Silence is not empty.  
It is mortar in the tyrant’s wall,  
a locked gate, a hand withdrawn.  
I have called my fear “strategy,”  
my weariness “wisdom,”  
my distance “neutrality.”  
But Heaven knows the names of things.

On these Days of Awe, I stand before the Book of Life  
with ink on my fingers and smoke in my clothes.  
The year burns behind me.  
The year ahead is dry grass.

May repentance be more than sorrow.  
May it become a door kicked open,  
a shield lifted,  
a voice that does not wait to be safe.

Seal us not only for life,  
but for courage—  
for the fierce, unfinished work  
of making life possible for one another.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short literary monologue beginning with “On the birthday of the world,” focused on moral accountability, political courage, and the desire to wield language as a weapon for change.
counterfactuals.output:
On the birthday of the world, I found my name written beneath every silence I had kept. No tyrant had forced my hand; no law had sealed my mouth. I had simply mistaken safety for innocence.

But conscience is a patient witness. It remembers the door we did not open, the lie we let pass as policy, the neighbor we reduced to a number. To live among others is to inherit a share of their wounds—and a duty to answer for the wounds we cause.

So let the powerful call courage disorder. Let them polish their speeches until injustice gleams like reason. I want no such eloquence. Give me words with edges. Give me sentences that break locks, questions that outlive prisons, names spoken clearly where erasure has done its work.

If language is the only weapon in my hand, I will sharpen it on truth. And if I must be judged, let it be for speaking too fiercely—not for arriving, once again, too late.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an impassioned spiritual reflection that blends repentance with resistance. The narrator should condemn their own complacency in a time of propaganda and shrinking freedoms, ending with a call for words capable of igniting action.
counterfactuals.output:
Forgive me for the silence I renamed prudence,  
for the comfort I mistook for peace.  
While lies marched brightly across every screen,  
I lowered my eyes and called it weariness.  
While freedoms narrowed—door by door, law by law—  
I thanked heaven that the walls had not yet reached my house.

I confess: I learned to live beside the alarm.  
I let outrage become ritual and grief become spectacle.  
I watched truth be bartered for slogans, neighbors reduced to enemies,  
and fear dressed in the robes of patriotism.  
I knew the hour was dark, yet guarded my small portion of light  
as though the soul could be saved alone.

God of the prophets, break this cowardly calm.  
Strip from me the innocence of the uninvolved.  
Teach me repentance that does not end in tears,  
but rises from its knees with open eyes and steady hands.  
Let remorse become courage; let prayer become presence;  
let faith refuse every throne built from humiliation and deceit.

I will not worship the machinery of inevitability.  
I will not call submission unity, censorship safety,  
or cruelty the necessary price of order.  
I will remember that every empire of falsehood depends  
on ordinary people agreeing to repeat its language.

So cleanse my tongue of borrowed lies.  
Give me words that expose without dehumanizing,  
that summon without commanding,  
that tell the frightened they are not alone  
and the complacent that neutrality has a cost.

Give us words with breath in them—  
words that pass from mouth to mouth like dawn,  
words that open locked doors, gather scattered hands,  
and ignite not hatred, but conscience;  
not chaos, but courage;  
not ashes, but action.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
